title: Workload-to-Hardware Fit & Scheduler Evaluation Guide
author: Priya Nair
content:
Overview
=======

This guide sets out a repeatable way to characterize production inference workloads, match them to accelerator classes, and evaluate scheduler and kernel policies so SLOs are met at the lowest reasonable cost. It brings together the profiling steps, benchmark harness setup, rollout acceptance criteria, common failure modes and short runbook actions for operations.

Goals
-----
- Build a deterministic workload fingerprint (latency shape, token density, sequence distribution, KV-cache affinity).
- Map fingerprints onto a small set of hardware classes (H100-80GB, A100-80GB, L40s-48GB, T4-16GB) with expected cost and tail-latency envelopes.
- Evaluate scheduler knobs (batching, slotting, preemption, kernel hints) and measure their effect on per-token cost, p50/p95/p99 latency and GPU utilization.
- Give a decision checklist for choosing model variants and fallback policies.

Scope and audience
------------------
For SREs, runtime engineers and applied ML engineers who handle model onboarding, canary design, Dedicated capacity sizing and private deployment sizing. Assumes working knowledge of trace-proxy, kernel-hint annotations and the benchmarking harness in tools/perf-harness.

Key definitions
---------------
- Request shape: fixed properties of a request - prompt tokens, response token cap, streaming or not.
- Sequence distribution: histogram of input+output lengths over a sample window.
- Affinity: likelihood that successive requests share KV cache entries (session/conversation affinity).
- Fidelity class: a model/quantization/profile combination with a known quality and cost.

1) Workload fingerprinting
--------------------------
Production-safe steps:
1. Choose a representative capture window (3-6 hours of normal traffic, or 24h per release). Prefer business hours plus a 24h weekend slice for consumer apps.
2. Shadow-capture requests with trace-proxy, side-effects disabled. Capture timestamp, user/session id, model, route, seq_len_in, seq_len_out_cap, kv_cache_hit_estimate, tokens_generated, latency_ms, error_code and kernel-hints. For high-volume routes write JSONL at 1k/s sampling.

Capture command:
```
trace-proxy capture --router $ROUTE --write /tmp/captures/$ROUTE-2025-08-05.jsonl --sample-rate 0.01 --fields timestamp,request_id,session_id,model,route,seq_in,seq_out_cap,kv_hint,latency_ms,error
```

Derived signals:
- tokens_per_request = seq_in + median(seq_out_observed if available else seq_out_cap)
- burstiness = distribution of request counts in 1s windows
- continuity_index = fraction of consecutive session requests on the same model/version

Output: workload-profile.json, the canonical perf-harness input. Example:
```
{
  "route": "search-completions",
  "time_window": "2025-08-05T08:00:00Z/2025-08-05T12:00:00Z",
  "seq_len_p50": "48",
  "seq_len_p95": "224",
  "tokens_p_request_avg": "132",
  "kv_affinity": "0.72",
  "burst_percentile_99": "34"
}
```

2) Benchmark matrix & experiment design
---------------------------------------
Cover hardware classes, model variants (fp16, q4_k, q8_0), kernel configurations (continuous batching on/off, slot size, preemption policy) and traffic shapes (steady, microburst, session-affine).

Minimum matrix for production acceptance:
- Hardware: {H100-80GB, A100-80GB, L40s-48GB}
- Model variants: {fp16, q4_k, q8_0}
- Scheduler presets: {latency-tilt, throughput-tilt, balanced}
- Traffic shapes: {baseline-day, microburst-peak, long-seq-synth}

Per run, record p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization (SM%, mem%), kernel queue length, kernel dispatch time histogram and an energy-per-token estimate.

Acceptance criteria (example):
- p99 <= declared SLO + 10% (safety buffer) on the latency-tilt config for the baseline-day shape.
- tokens/sec per GPU within 10% of the committed reserve for Dedicated customers.
- Model quality: the automatic eval set shows BLEU/ROUGE/semantic-similarity delta below the defined threshold.

3) Scheduler & kernel evaluation checklist
-----------------------------------------
Knobs to sweep:
- batch_size_max: kernel overhead amortization vs tail latency. Sweep 1, 4, 8, 16 for short sequences.
- batch_wait_ms: latency/throughput trade-off for bursty traffic.
- preemption_policy: eager | cooperative | disabled. Use cooperative on multi-tenant pools.
- slot_quota / tenant_credits: fairness under contention.
- kernel_hint: fused_attention | sharded_attention | memory_opt, to select specialized kernels.

Evaluator actions:
1. Run a low-load baseline to find the kernel latency floor per kernel_hint.
2. Add mixed-priority synthetic load to measure priority inversion and starvation.
3. Toggle preemption to weigh warm-start cost against p99 gains.
4. Measure the KV-cache warmup curve (cold -> 30m -> 2h) to estimate steady-state savings.

Example result rows:
"Hardware | Kernel_hint | batch_size | p50 | p95 | p99 | tokens/s | SM% | Notes"
"H100 | fused_attention_v2 | 8 | 22ms | 48ms | 120ms | 4200 | 73% | Best for long seqs"

4) Profiling recipe (trace to remediation)
-----------------------------------------
Trigger: p99 regression or a new kernel rollout.

First 20 minutes:
1. Establish scope: affected routes, time window, customer impact (kibana/route-dashboard).
2. Pull the route's canonical workload-profile. A >10% change in seq_len_p95 or burstiness counts as a traffic-shift.
3. Raise trace-proxy sampling on the affected route to 1%.
4. Correlate trace IDs with runtime kernel traces to find slow kernels:
  - kernel-trace aggregate --start TS1 --end TS2 --group-by kernel_hint --metric mean_dispatch_ms,p95_dispatch_ms
5. Dispatch time up with SM% flat -> likely kernel regression (new codepath or compilation change).
6. SM% and memory pressure both up -> likely higher concurrency or larger batches; check eviction logs.

Common remediations:
- Roll back the kernel via feature flag: runtime-flag set kernel_selector=stable
- Memory pressure: lower batch_size_max and enable eager-eviction for ephemeral caches
- Priority inversion: temporarily raise tenant_credits for the route or grant an emergency quota exemption for critical traffic

5) Cost & capacity guidance
---------------------------
Inputs:
- tokens_per_request (from the fingerprint)
- tokens_per_second_per_GPU (from the benchmark)
- cloud GPU $/hr (procurement table)
- target utilization (60–70% for Dedicated pools)

Formula:
"Provisioned GPUs = ceil(peak_tokens_per_sec / tokens_per_second_per_GPU / target_utilization)"

Example: 500k tokens/sec required, 4k tokens/sec per GPU, target_util 0.65 -> GPUs = ceil(500000 / 4000 / 0.65) = 193 GPUs

6) Canary and rollout matrix for scheduler/kernel changes
--------------------------------------------------------
Principles:
- Small, fast canaries: 1% traffic for 15 minutes with full tracing.
- Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%, checking p99/p95 and per-route cost at each step.
- Safety gates: automatic rollback if p99 increases >30% or tokens/sec drops >15% vs baseline.

Telemetry to watch:
- route-p99, route-error-rate, kernel-dispatch-p95, gpu-eviction-rate, kv-warmup-slope.

Canary checklist:
1. Start at 1% for 15m, review traces and run the profiling recipe.
2. If checks pass, go to 5% for 1h and run the full benchmark matrix in that period.
3. If a safety gate trips, revert to the previous kernel_selector and escalate to runtime-oncall.

7) Known issues
---------------
- Large-LLM microbursts exhausting slots: use per-route burst_alloc and shorter batch windows.
- KV-cache skew across shards: scale-up drains raise cold hits; stagger cache warms on scale events.
- GPU memory fragmentation after quantization rollouts: run a compaction job in maintenance windows.

8) Runbook extracts
-------------------
Symptom: sudden p99 increase on route X
- Pager owner: runtime-oncall
- Within 10 minutes:
  1. Confirm impact (p99 spike above the configured alert threshold).
  2. Check deploy-log and trace-capture for a deployment or traffic-shift correlation.
  3. If a deployment correlates, flip kernel_selector to the previous stable tag and watch for 10m.
  4. If it is a traffic-shift, apply emergency throttles or a temporary scaling policy to the Dedicated pool.
  5. Open an incident ticket with kernel traces and assign the oncall engineer.

Symptom: GPU OOMs during rollout
- Steps:
  1. Pause the rollout.
  2. Cut batch_size_max by 50% on the affected pool.
  3. Start compaction: gpu-mem-compact --pool $POOL --max-run 2h
  4. Escalate to infra-gpu if OOMs continue.

9) Release notes template
-------------------------
- Release tag: x.y.z
- Owners: runtime-team
- Summary: one sentence on user-facing impact
- Benchmarks run: hardware, routes, model variants
- Canary plan: percentages + safety gates
- Known limitations: e.g. T4 behaviour on long sequences
- Rollback steps: commands and feature-flag names
- Artifacts: workload-profile(s) and perf-harness logs

10) Ownership and links
-----------------------
- Owners: runtime-team (oncall rotation), perf-engineering for the harness, infra-gpu for hardware incidents.
- Links:
  - perf-harness repo: //git.internal/redwood/perf-harness
  - canonical workload storage: s3://redwood-perf/workloads/

Appendices
----------
A. Example scheduler policy (YAML)
```
policy_name: latency-tilt-small-batches
batching:
  max_batch_size: 8
  batch_wait_ms: 6
preemption:
  policy: cooperative
  preempt_check_interval_ms: 50
quota:
  tenant_credit_mode: burstable
  default_quota_tokens_per_minute: 60000
kernel_hints:
  preferred: [fused_attention_v2, sharded_attention]
```

B. Profiling commands
- Kernel traces for a window:
```
kernel-trace aggregate --route search-completions --start 2025-08-05T08:00:00Z --end 2025-08-05T09:00:00Z --out /tmp/kt.json
```
- Synthetic microburst generator:
```
perf-harness loadgen --profile workload-profile.json --shape microburst --duration 15m --out /tmp/run-01
```
